walkthrough:
Name the Five Bases Correctly**
You are sitting with the two pairing rules you know well. In DNA, A pairs with T and C pairs with G. That gives adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine. RNA uses the same except U replaces T, giving uracil. Spelling matters for the mark, so learn: adenine, cytosine, guanine, thymine, uracil.

Sort Purines from Pyrimidines by Rings**
Think structure determines category. Purines are bigger with a double ring made of a 6-membered ring fused to a 5-membered ring. Only adenine and guanine are purines. Pyrimidines are smaller with a single 6-membered ring. Cytosine, thymine and uracil are pyrimidines.

Sort DNA, RNA or Both**
A, C and G are common to both DNA and RNA, so write both. T is found only in DNA. U is found only in RNA. That completes all three columns for full marks.
Final answer: A = adenine, purine, both; C = cytosine, pyrimidine, both; G = guanine, purine, both; T = thymine, pyrimidine, DNA; U = uracil, pyrimidine, RNA.

hints: Look closely at the nitrogen-containing base part of carbovir triphosphate in Fig. 5.1. Count how many rings are fused together in that base.
walkthrough:
Count the Rings to Identify the Base Type**
Look at the right-hand molecule in Fig. 5.1. Its base has a 6-membered ring fused to a 5-membered ring, so two rings joined together. That is the defining feature of a purine, just like adenine and guanine. Pyrimidines have only one ring, so this cannot be a pyrimidine analogue.
Final answer: Purine, as it has a double ring / two-ring structure similar to adenine / guanine.

hints: Compare the left and right molecules in Fig. 5.1. What new chemical group has been added to abacavir to make carbovir triphosphate?
Recall what DNA polymerase normally does - what form of nucleotide does it add to the elongating chain, and why would a triphosphate be a better mimic than a nucleoside?
walkthrough:
Spot the Change from Nucleoside to Nucleotide**
Abacavir on the left has base plus sugar-like ring but no phosphate, so it is like a nucleoside. Carbovir triphosphate on the right has three phosphates attached, so it is now like an activated nucleotide. The small triangular cyclopropyl group is also lost.

Link to What DNA Polymerase Expects**
DNA polymerase does not join nucleosides. Its normal substrates are activated nucleotides (dNTPs) which it adds to the 3-prime end of the elongating chain, forming phosphodiester bonds and hydrogen bonds to the complementary base on the template. Because carbovir triphosphate now looks like a real activated purine nucleotide, it fits the active site much better and is more likely to be accepted and added.

Final answer: Carbovir triphosphate has three phosphates / is phosphorylated / activated so is a nucleotide analogue, not a nucleoside; it is therefore similar to the activated DNA nucleotides that are substrates for DNA polymerase added to the growing chain / forming phosphodiester bonds.

hints: Start with shape. If carbovir triphosphate looks like the normal nucleotide substrate, where in the enzyme will it go?
Think about competition. What happens to normal enzyme-substrate complexes when an analogue occupies the active site?
Consider what happens after it is inserted. Can DNA polymerase continue to add the next nucleotide and form normal phosphodiester bonds?
Finish the causal chain to viral DNA. What is the overall effect on elongation and production of complete viral DNA?
walkthrough:
Mimicry Lets It Bind the Active Site**
Enzymes work by complementary shape between active site and substrate. Because carbovir triphosphate is very similar in shape to a normal activated purine nucleotide, it can fit into and bind the active site of viral DNA polymerase.

Act as an Inhibitor by Competition**
Once in the active site it acts as an inhibitor, often competitive. It competes with real DNA nucleotides for the site, so fewer enzyme molecules are available to bind the correct substrate and fewer normal enzyme-substrate complexes form. It may bind irreversibly or alter the tertiary / 3D shape of the enzyme.

Block Elongation After Insertion**
Carbovir triphosphate can be inserted into the growing polynucleotide chain. Its sugar-like part is not normal deoxyribose, so DNA polymerase cannot form the next phosphodiester bond correctly and cannot add further nucleotides. The polymerase may stall, detach from the template, or produce faulty DNA that is broken down.

Prevent Complete Viral DNA Synthesis**
If the chain cannot elongate, full-length viral DNA is never completed and cannot be further replicated. Without its genome copied, the virus cannot make new infectious particles. That is how the drug stops viral multiplication.

Final answer: Similar / complementary shape to nucleotide substrate so binds to active site of DNA polymerase as inhibitor / competes with DNA nucleotides, reducing ES complexes; incorporated into growing chain then prevents further addition of nucleotides / prevents phosphodiester bond formation, so chain cannot elongate and complete viral DNA is not made.
